extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/history of science and readers of Bacon's Novum Organum (those studying scientific method and induction)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explaining Bacon's methodological categories (prerogative instances and related auxiliaries) and his preliminary vindication/definition of heat as presented in the Novum Organum with examples and cautions. Focuses on types of decisive instances and auxiliaries used to discover and test forms in natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praerogativae Instantiarum (Prerogative Instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristic phenomena selected from the mass of facts because, by their number, indistinctness, and complication, they would otherwise confuse rather than direct the mind; phenomena that strikingly and forcibly indicate a nature and thus demand first attention in physical enquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These instances are chosen because a few of them can do the work of many: they remove ambiguities and accelerate induction. They are to be used first in enquiry and are discussed with reference to their practical utility (see Herschel, Playfair). They form part of the 'inquisitionis contractio'—a method of selecting short, decisive paths through complicated evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adminicula Inductionis (Auxiliaries of Induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the principal auxiliaries to be applied after the tables and primary eliminations; auxiliary aids that assist the intellect in interpretation and in conducting induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the second major division of aids to induction (to be elaborated where needed). The 'ulteriora auxilia' are intended to perfect the Exclusiva (exclusive eliminations) because the tables alone are not supposed to be sufficient. Practical utility would be explained in connection with prerogative instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectificatio Inductionis (Rectification of Induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A named auxiliary of the inquiry process concerned with correcting and improving inductive reasoning and results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given as the third major heading in the methodological plan; intended to be applied after initial tables and prerogative instances. (The text enumerates it among the necessary parts of a complete inquisition but does not fully expand it in this chunk.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Variatio Inquisitionis pro Natura Subjecti (Variation of Inquiry for the Subject's Nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A methodological heading concerning how to vary the inquiry according to the particular nature under examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the fourth division — signals that the mode of experiment and comparison should be adapted to the subject's character. The text later treats different kinds of instances (solitary, migrating, ostensive) as part of this tailored variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praerogativae Naturarum quatenus ad inquisitionem (Prerogatives of Natures with Respect to Inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: An intended systematic enumeration (sixth division) of the simple or principal natures, arranged perhaps in a hierarchy according to their relative importance for investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the full methodological scheme; the author contemplates exhaustively enumerating important simple natures so that their prerogative value to inquiry is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminis Inquisitionis (Terms of Inquiry / Synopses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A heading for a synoptic summary of the whole inquisition — terms and definitions that frame the inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the sixth/seventh item in the methodological outline; intended to provide concise terminological and conceptual scaffolding for the inductive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductio ad Praxin (Deduction to Practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The part of the method concerned with deduction directed toward human use (practical application of discovered forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named as the seventh division — the step translating discovered forms and axioms into practical operations and technologies. It follows the discovery phases and is explicitly included in the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parasceveis ad Inquisitionem (Preparations/Parasceves for Inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary materials and preparations necessary for carrying out the inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among the structural parts of the methodological program (e.g., 'Parasceve' tract mentioned). Intended to be considered in due order as part of the inquisition; further elaboration appears elsewhere in Bacon's works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scala Ascensoria et Descensoria Axiomatum (Ascending and Descending Scale of Axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed hierarchical ordering (scale) of axioms that supports ascent and descent in reasoning from instances to axioms and back to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given as the final part of the methodological plan, indicating the intention to organize axioms so they support both induction (ascending) and deduction/practice (descending).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Solitariae (Solitary Instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that exhibit the nature under investigation in subjects which have nothing in common with other subjects save that nature, or conversely instances in which the nature is absent in subjects otherwise alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: to remove ambiguities and to accelerate and strengthen exclusive induction; a few such instances can be as effective as many. They correspond to the Method of Agreement (and, in the second division, the Method of Difference). Examples: prisms and crystalline gems that render colours both in themselves and externally; distinct white and black veins in marble; variegations in flowers — these share only colour and thus indicate colour as a modification of light rather than an intrinsic property of those materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Migrantes (Travelling or Migrating Instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances in which the nature under investigation 'migrates' — appears (generation) where it did not before, or vanishes (corruption) where it did; includes gradations toward increase and decrease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics: such instances are often twin (one at a stage and one at the opposite stage) and press the affirmative (they help to pin down the form). They are very useful for the operative part (they suggest praxis) because they show form coupled with efficient causes. Caution: do not confuse the efficient cause with the form itself; the efficient may be merely the vehicle for the form. Examples: intact glass vs pulverized glass (diaphanous -> white), simple water vs foamed water (diaphanous -> white), papyrus dry (white) vs wet (less white/closer to diaphanous). Such instances can indicate how form is transferred or removed by comminution or inclusion of air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Ostensive / Elucescentiae (Ostensive or Illuminating Instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that display the nature under investigation in a naked, substantive, and exalted state — liberated from impediments and dominant over other coupled forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: to reveal the nature when it is otherwise obscured by other forms present in the concrete. These powerful instances suppress or coerce interfering forms and thus make the sought nature manifest in its full potency. They are especially valuable where multiple forms in a subject obscure one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima Vindemiatio / Definition of the Form of Heat (Forma Calidi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon's preliminary interpretive definition (Prima Vindemiatio) of heat in itself (not merely as felt by the senses): 'Calor est motus expansivus, cohibitus, et nitens per partes minores.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further modifications given: expansion is all-round with slight tendency upward; motion occurs in smaller particles (not to ultimate fineness but 'quasi-majusculae'); the motion is restrained and repulsed and often tremulous or oscillatory; the sense-perceived 'warmth' is analogous to but modified from the form in itself. Examples and experimental notes: flame and boiling liquids show tremor and local tumescence; heated iron shows strong heat without obvious bulk expansion; heat is propagated by convection and conduction (note on Tyndall). The editor warns Bacon's theory sometimes outstrips his proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative designation for producing heat
rubrics_metrics.description: An operative (operativa) prescription: if in any natural body you can excite motion tending to dilate or expand it, and so restrain and convert that motion that the dilation does not proceed equally but is partly checked and partly driven back, you will generate heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a testable experimental rule applicable regardless of whether the material is elementary, celestial, luminous, opaque, thin, dense, localized, or mobile. Examples/implications: friction/stoppage producing lasting heat; confinement and unequal exposure producing warming; the rule indicates experimental approaches to produce heat by creating unequal expansion in parts of a body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Differentia of Heat: motion by smaller particles and tremor
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat is not a uniform expansion of the whole but expansion acting through smaller 'particles' of the body, accompanied by restraint, repulsion and continual trembling or oscillation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifest in flame and boiling liquids (perpetual tremor and local swelling), in bodies with compact cohesion (heated iron not visibly swelling), and in the fact that cold weather can intensify burning. The editor notes an anticipation of the undulatory theory of heat but also criticises that Bacon's collected instances are often of little value in proving the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth Differentia of Heat: rapidity and particle-size qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: The stimulative or penetrative motion constituting heat must be somewhat rapid and not very slow; it operates through particles that are minute but not to the utmost fineness ('quasi-majusculae').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to distinguish the effects of heat from the effects of time/age, which can produce dissolution more finely and more slowly so as not to be perceived as 'heat.' Example: gold dissolves without excited heat, iron dissolves with strong excitation of heat because of greater obstinacy of its parts. This qualification is noted as erroneous in some passages but is discussed as Bacon's attempt to delimit the nature of heat.
